description: Bartlett's reconstructive memory theory, War of the Ghosts study, and factors that distort recall.
content_html:
Memory as an Active Process

You might assume that remembering is like playing back a recording — a faithful replay of what happened. But psychologists have found that memory is far more active than this. When we recall something, we do not simply read it out from storage; we actively reconstruct it, filling in gaps using our existing knowledge, expectations, and beliefs. This process can lead to errors, distortions, and even entirely false memories.

Bartlett’s Theory of Reconstructive Memory

Frederick Bartlett argued that memory is not a passive copy of the past but an active process of reconstruction. He proposed the concept of schema — a mental framework of knowledge built up from past experience. When we recall something, we use our schemas to fill in the gaps, making the memory fit what we “expect” to be true rather than what actually happened. Bartlett called this tendency effort after meaning: we work to make our memories logical and coherent, even if that means unconsciously altering them.

Key Fact

Bartlett’s Theory of Reconstructive Memory proposes that recall is an active reconstruction shaped by schemas and the effort after meaning. This explains why our recollections often change over time, filling in gaps to match what we expect rather than what actually occurred.

Bartlett’s War of the Ghosts Study

Bartlett tested his theory using a story called “The War of the Ghosts,” a Native American folk tale unfamiliar to his British participants. He chose this story deliberately because it contained cultural elements and a narrative logic that would be foreign to British readers, so any changes in retelling would reveal how schemas distort memory.

Key Fact

Bartlett’s War of the Ghosts study: Aim — to investigate how memory for an unfamiliar story changes over time. Method — British participants read the story and recalled it repeatedly over intervals ranging from hours to years. Results — participants altered, shortened and rationalised the story to fit familiar cultural expectations; unfamiliar elements were omitted or replaced. Conclusion — memory is an active reconstruction shaped by prior knowledge and schemas, not a faithful replay.

A strength of Bartlett’s study is its ecological validity — participants recalled a meaningful story rather than an artificial list of words, which is closer to real-world memory tasks. The repeated recall method also reveals how memory changes over time, which has practical implications for eyewitness testimony.

A weakness is that Bartlett’s methods were not tightly controlled. The story was not standardised in all versions, and Bartlett did not use statistical analysis — he relied on qualitative descriptions of changes. This makes it harder to replicate precisely and limits how confidently we can draw general conclusions from his data.

Factors Affecting the Accuracy of Memory

Beyond schemas, three specific factors can distort what we remember: interference, context, and false memories. Each operates differently, but all demonstrate that memory is not a fixed record.

Interference

Interference occurs when one memory makes another harder to recall or distorts it. There are two types. Proactive interference is when an older memory disrupts recall of a newer one — for example, if you have previously learned Spanish, it may interfere with learning Italian. Retroactive interference is when a newer memory disrupts recall of an older one — for example, if you learn a new phone number, it may make you more likely to forget your old one.

Context

Memory is also affected by context. Research has shown that memory is better when the conditions at retrieval match the conditions during encoding. This is known as context-dependent memory. For example, information learned in a particular room may be recalled more easily when you return to that room. Internal states can also act as context: if you encode a memory while in a particular emotional state, you may recall it more easily when you return to that state.

False Memories

False memories are recollections of events that either never happened or are substantially different from how they actually occurred. They can arise from post-event misinformation, suggestion from others, or the natural reconstructive processes Bartlett described. False memories feel just as real to the person holding them as genuine ones, which has significant implications for eyewitness testimony in legal settings.

Understanding that memory is reconstructive has important real-world implications. Eyewitness testimony is less reliable than courts once assumed, because witnesses unconsciously alter their memories using schemas, are affected by leading questions (post-event information), and may form false memories. Research in this area has influenced how police conduct interviews and how courts evaluate eyewitness evidence.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about Bartlett, make sure you use the correct term: ‘reconstructive memory’, not ‘reconstructed’ or ‘reconstructing.’ For the study description, link the results (changes in retelling) directly to the conclusion (schemas distort recall) rather than just listing the findings. On 9-mark questions, evaluate by contrasting Bartlett’s approach with more controlled studies: his ecological validity is a strength but his lack of statistical analysis is a weakness — always elaborate on WHY each is a strength or weakness.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bartlett’s Theory of Reconstructive Memory proposes that recall is an active process shaped by schemas and effort after meaning, not a faithful playback of past events.
  • Bartlett’s War of the Ghosts study showed that British participants altered, shortened and rationalised an unfamiliar Native American story over repeated retelling, demonstrating schema-driven distortion.
  • Three key factors that affect memory accuracy are interference (competing memories), context (better recall when retrieval conditions match encoding conditions), and false memories (recollections of events that did not occur or were distorted).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'effort after meaning'?
A) Trying hard to recall every detail of an event
B) Distorting information to fit existing knowledge and make it seem logical
C) Using a memory cue to trigger recall of a forgotten item
D) Repeating information to transfer it from STM to LTM
practice_questions.marks: B) Distorting information to fit existing knowledge and make it seem logical [1 mark]

Mastering: Precise definition stating that a false memory is a recollection of an event that did not actually occur, or a significantly distorted memory of one that did, arising from reconstructive processes or post-event suggestion.
Secure: Clear definition capturing the idea of remembering something inaccurate or imagined.
Developing: Partial definition — may say ‘imagining something happened’ without linking to memory processes.
Emerging: Vague attempt such as ‘a wrong memory.’

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a schema and explain how schemas can distort memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines schema as a mental framework of knowledge built from past experience; explains that during recall, schemas fill in gaps with expected information rather than actual details; links to effort after meaning or Bartlett’s theory; uses accurate terminology.
Secure: Defines schema and gives a developed explanation of how it causes distortion.
Developing: Defines schema or explains distortion, but not both clearly.
Emerging: Vague reference to knowledge or memory without linking the two.

practice_questions.text: Describe Bartlett's War of the Ghosts study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Aim (investigate how memory for unfamiliar story changes over time), method (British participants read and recalled a Native American folk tale over varying intervals), results (participants shortened, rationalised and changed the story to fit familiar cultural schemas; unfamiliar details omitted or replaced), conclusion (memory is active reconstruction shaped by prior knowledge) — all four elements present, precise language used.
Secure: All four elements present; one may lack full development.
Developing: Three elements present; one missing or inaccurate.
Emerging: Only the results or a vague gist of the study; structure not evident.

practice_questions.text: Jaya witnessed a car accident and later told police what she saw. A week later, her account had changed: she remembered a red car being involved, even though there was no red car. Use Bartlett's Theory of Reconstructive Memory to explain why Jaya's memory changed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies reconstructive memory and schemas; explains that Jaya’s recall was shaped by her prior knowledge and expectations (schemas) about what accidents look like; effort after meaning led her to fill in gaps with plausible details; links directly to the scenario (adding a red car).
Secure: Correct identification of reconstructive memory with clear scenario engagement.
Developing: Names reconstructive memory or schemas but explanation limited or only loosely linked to Jaya’s account.
Emerging: Identifies that memory can be wrong without using Bartlett’s framework.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Bartlett's Theory of Reconstructive Memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Memory is active reconstruction shaped by schemas and effort after meaning; we fill in gaps to make memories coherent; supported by War of the Ghosts study — participants altered and shortened an unfamiliar story over time. Three factors affecting accuracy: interference, context, false memories.
Evaluation (AO3): Strength — ecological validity; using a story is closer to real-world memory than word lists. Strength — practical applications; understanding of reconstructive memory has influenced eyewitness testimony research and police interview techniques. Weakness — lack of controlled methodology; Bartlett did not use standardised procedures or statistical analysis. Weakness — theory does not explain all types of memory error; some highly accurate ‘flashbulb’ memories suggest memory is not always distorted.
Mastering: Accurate, detailed description and at least two developed evaluation points with elaboration.
Secure: Description and two evaluation points with some elaboration.
Developing: Description and one evaluation point.
Emerging: Brief description; evaluation absent or undeveloped.

knowledge_checks.q: What does Bartlett's concept of 'effort after meaning' describe?
options: Working hard to recall as many details as possible
Distorting unfamiliar information to fit existing knowledge
Using the effort of rehearsal to transfer memories to LTM
Searching for a retrieval cue when recall fails

knowledge_checks.q: In Bartlett's War of the Ghosts study, what happened to the story over repeated retellings?
options: Participants recalled it more accurately each time
The story stayed largely the same across retellings
Participants shortened and rationalised the story, omitting unfamiliar details
Participants added more detail and made the story longer

knowledge_checks.q: Bartlett argued that memory is not a passive replay but an active process of _____.
When a newer memory disrupts recall of an older one, this is called _____ interference.
Match each factor to how it affects memory accuracy:
right: Recollections of events that never occurred or were distorted
When conditions at recall match those at encoding, memory improves
Competing memories reduce the accuracy of recall

flashcard_questions.q: What does Bartlett's Theory of Reconstructive Memory argue about recall?
flashcard_questions.a: That recall is an active reconstruction, not a faithful playback of stored events.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a schema in psychology?
flashcard_questions.a: A mental framework of knowledge built from past experience, used to interpret and reconstruct information.
The tendency to distort unfamiliar information to fit existing knowledge and make it seem logical.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the aim of Bartlett's War of the Ghosts study?
flashcard_questions.a: To investigate how memory for an unfamiliar story changes over time.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Bartlett use a Native American folk tale for his study?
flashcard_questions.a: It was culturally unfamiliar to British participants, so schema-driven changes would be detectable.

flashcard_questions.q: What were Bartlett's results in the War of the Ghosts study?
flashcard_questions.a: Participants shortened and rationalised the story, omitting or replacing unfamiliar details.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Bartlett's conclusion from the War of the Ghosts study?
flashcard_questions.a: Memory is an active reconstruction shaped by prior knowledge, not a faithful replay.
When one memory disrupts or competes with another, reducing accuracy of recall.
Better recall when conditions at retrieval match conditions during encoding.
A memory of an event that did not happen, or a significantly distorted version of one that did.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one strength of Bartlett's War of the Ghosts study.
flashcard_questions.a: Higher ecological validity than word-list studies, as participants recalled a meaningful story.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one weakness of Bartlett's study.
flashcard_questions.a: Lack of standardised procedures and no statistical analysis, limiting precise replication.

glossary_terms.definition: The active process of rebuilding a memory at the point of recall, often filling in gaps with expectations and existing knowledge.
A mental framework of knowledge and expectations based on prior experience, used to interpret and reconstruct new information.
The tendency to make sense of unfamiliar information by distorting it to fit existing knowledge and expectations.
When one memory disrupts or competes with another, reducing the accuracy or availability of the targeted memory.
The environmental or internal cues present during encoding; recall is better when the context at retrieval matches the context at encoding.
A memory of an event that did not actually happen, or a significantly distorted memory of one that did.

hero_image_caption: Memory works like a jigsaw puzzle reconstructed from fragments, not a photograph.
